sections.html:
Down in the Lowcountry of southern South Carolina, Beaufort County borders Colleton, Jasper and Hampton counties. Water makes up roughly 37.6 percent of its 923.48 square miles, which is why marsh, rivers and the Atlantic decide where houses can go. The 2025 estimate is 204,433 residents, compared with 187,117 in the 2020 Census, when about 76,373 households were counted.

Hilton Head Island is the biggest community and the city of Beaufort holds the county seat. Bluffton and Port Royal are municipalities too, along with parts of Yemassee and Hardeeville. A house on an island, by a marsh or in a planned community can sit in a different tax district from the one next door. The Auditor's website has a Tax District Locator and a Tax Calculator for checking.

Property tax passes through three hands. The Auditor creates the notices using the millage that the county and each municipality set. The Treasurer mails them and takes payment. The Assessor places the value on real property and processes the legal residence application.

Beaufort County property tax offices
OfficePhoneHandles
Assessor, 100 Ribaut Road, Room 210, Beaufort(843) 255-2400Values, appeals, the 4 percent residence rate
Auditor(843) 255-2500Notices and the senior homestead exemption for ages 65 and up
Treasurer(843) 341-8404Payment, installments, delinquent taxes, tax sales

Online payment goes through myBeaufortCounty.com, where the Treasurer's Tax Document Lookup also shows original bills and paid receipts.

Auditor counters exist in Beaufort (100 Ribaut Road) and Bluffton (4819 Bluffton Parkway). They keep Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Friday hours of 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., and Wednesday starts later: 9:00 a.m. in Beaufort, 10:00 a.m. in Bluffton.

January 15 is the due date. Anything postmarked afterward is penalized: state law adds 3 percent, then 7 percent more from February 2, then 5 percent more from March 17, and finally the bill goes out for execution.

Beware the postmark. It may show when the mail was processed, which is not necessarily when you dropped the envelope in the box. The office can forgive a penalty in narrow situations, such as documented proof that USPS accepted the mail on time or a confirmed county error. The safest habit is to mail several days ahead or to have a post office clerk apply a manual postmark.

When a property is sold during the year and the buyer received no notice, state law has the treasurer waive the penalties. For a sale within the current year, pass the notice to the new owner or call the closing attorney.

Beaufort's most recent reassessment took effect in 2023, and the following one is expected in 2028. State law mandates a countywide reappraisal every fifth year.

To contest a value you can pick one of two routes:

  • File any time from January 1 of the current year up to January 15 of the next year.
  • Or file within 90 days after an assessment notice reaches you.

Choosing both in a single tax year is not allowed. The assessor replies, and then 30 days are available to appeal to the county board of assessment appeals. If the board rules against you, another 30 days let you ask for a hearing at the Administrative Law Court.

sections.h2: What a sale does to the assessment
sections.html:
Most sales are an assessable transfer of interest, appraised as of December 31 of the year of transfer. The 4 percent rate for a primary residence has to be requested by the owner, and the Assessor takes those requests from January 1 of the current year through January 15 of the next. A buyer who does not ask is billed at 6 percent.

An ATI exemption is also offered. It can lower the fair market value by up to 25 percent, never below the current county record value, and the property is assessed at 6 percent in the year it is granted. The application is due before January 31 of the first tax year you qualify, and the Assessor can say whether your sale is eligible.

A sale lets you settle unpaid taxes at closing, and that is usually easier than waiting for a tax sale to happen. If a delinquent tax sale does occur, the defaulting owner, a grantee, or a mortgage or judgment creditor may redeem for twelve months by paying taxes, penalties and costs plus interest, which grows from 3 percent in the first quarter to 12 percent in the last.

Request a payoff from the Treasurer that is good through your closing date and give it to the closing attorney. If you want to know how a current-year bill will be divided between buyer and seller, raise that before the contract is signed.

Cash Home Buyers purchases Beaufort County houses in their current condition, including inherited homes and rentals, and the closing attorney deals with the tax payoff. Send us the address and the most recent notice and we will go over it with you.

sections.h2: Getting ready to sell in Beaufort County
sections.html:
First, the paperwork. Locate your latest tax bill, find out which tax district the house belongs to, and note the due date. For a rental or an inherited home, confirm who has been receiving the mail. Then contact the Treasurer for a payoff, and the Assessor with any question about value or the residence rate.

Hilton Head and Bluffton lie south of the Broad River and the city of Beaufort and Port Royal lie north of it, and buyers in each half shop differently. Tell the closing attorney early which half your house is in so the right offices are contacted. After closing, the buyer should apply for the 4 percent rate if they will live there.

On closing day, the closing attorney pulls together the payoff letter, the tax receipt and the settlement statement. Confirm that the payoff covers taxes, penalties and costs through the closing date, and that any open current-year bill is split the way your contract says. Ask for a copy of the final statement that shows the tax payment.

If the sale falls near January 15, check whether the new year's bill has gone out and who will pay it. If it falls after that date, ask whether penalty steps are already adding to the balance. Keep the closing statement, the payoff letter and any receipt with its postmark in one folder, so that a later notice can be answered quickly.

Give the buyer your forwarding address, and tell them to update the mailing address with the Treasurer and the Auditor so future bills reach the right person.

faqs.q: When are Beaufort County, SC property taxes due?
faqs.a: Mid-January, specifically January 15. A payment postmarked later is penalized, so mail early or pay online at myBeaufortCounty.com.

faqs.q: Which office do I call about my Beaufort County tax bill?
faqs.a: The Treasurer, (843) 341-8404, for payment. The Auditor, (843) 255-2500, for notices and homestead. The Assessor, (843) 255-2400, for value or the 4 percent residence rate.

faqs.q: How soon should a Beaufort County buyer apply for the 4 percent rate?
faqs.a: From January 1 of the current year through January 15 of the following year. A home that is not approved is billed at the higher 6 percent rate.

faqs.q: How long do I have to object to a Beaufort County assessment?
faqs.a: Either 90 days from the date of an assessment notice, or from January 1 through January 15 of the following year. The two options cannot be combined in one tax year.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Beaufort County house with tax unpaid?
faqs.a: Yes. Your closing attorney can pay the taxes and penalties from the proceeds, using a payoff from the Treasurer that is good through closing.
